utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. From amongst the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Ostojic. That's about it. Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. We still need to go through the exhibit tendering process in relation to yesterday's witness. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. We just have two items to tender from yesterday's testimony. The first is PIC 00137. That is the marked version of map 6 from the map book that the witness marked up yesterday. The second exhibit is PIC 00138. That is an aerial image of the Kravica warehouse, 65 ter P01563 marked by the witness yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it there are no objections from any of the Defence teams. There shouldn't be. So those two documents are admitted and the exhibit number will be verified, as you put it, Mr. Thayer, and confirmed later. The Defence, Mr. Stojanovic, I understand you have one document to tender; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. That's correct. We would like to tender the map that the witness marked yesterday. 4DIC 139 is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From any of the other Defence teams? None. Okay. So that is admitted. Number to be verified and confirmed. I take it there are no other exhibits. So before we bring in the next witness, we had an indication yesterday from Mr. McCloskey that a motion would be filed. At the time we were given the impression that it will deal with two persons but as it is, it only deals with this next witness, Witness 144. The request is that the protective measure he enjoyed in Blagojevic, that being of facial distortion, is made applicable also for the purpose of his evidence and his testimony in this case. Any objection from any of the Defence teams? None? So motion is granted. And Witness 144 will enjoy the protective measure of face distortion throughout his entire testimony. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was able to speak to the second witness yesterday late afternoon, and he asked the same thing. We didn't have time to get that into a -- the motion but I can file that this morning or we can do it orally, whatever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And since I know nothing about this other person, did he testify before?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, he did. It's another excavator operator in the previous case, in the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And did he enjoy any protective measures then?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was the same as this person. He was -- all he wanted was face distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we might try to avoid you having to file a written motion. Are you in a position, Defence teams, to agree to protective measures being placed also with regard to the other witness, that being limited to facial distortion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I take it there are no objections from any of the Defence teams. So you don't need to file a motion. We take what you stated as amounting to an oral request, an oral motion, which is also being granted already. So the next witness who would be number 146, will testify with the protective measure of facial distortion on. Okay. Any other submission before the witness comes in?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I mentioned yesterday, Mr. Lazarevic and I had a chance to speak, and we'll be speaking to you briefly on that point. We can do it after these witnesses or before, because it appears that we'll need a decision from you on the issue of playing the tape of Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's bring the witness in, please. And we'll try to allow some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this witness needs a caution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I was going to ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as a 92 bis with cross-examination witness, he now reverts to a 92 ter witness and I don't plan on asking him any questions and I do not have a summary, though I can give you a brief summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the summary we had imposed as a matter of rule, sort of, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can raise the curtains in the meantime. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are going to start giving evidence very soon, and before you do that, and you're familiar with this procedure because you've testified already, you are required to make a solemn declaration to us that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth. The text is being handed to you now. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. There are another few things I need to tell you before you start giving evidence. First one relates to a right that every witness that comes to testify before this Tribunal enjoys, in terms of our rules. It's not something that we have invented. It's something that exists in almost all jurisdictions that I am aware of. And it relates to witnesses' right against self-incrimination. Let me explain it to you in lay terms. There may be questions put to you, either from the Prosecution or from the Defence, that, if you would answer truthfully, could expose you to criminal proceedings. In other words, there could be what is sometimes referred to as incriminatory questions. In such a case, and I'm not saying that there will be such questions but there could be, in such a case, you have a right to ask for our protection, and ask us, the Trial Chamber, to exempt you from answering such questions. I say you have a right but it is not an absolute right. And it is not an absolute right because we can take either of two decisions: Either to exempt you from answering such questions, or to compel you to answer such questions notwithstanding your wish, your desire, not to. If we compel you to answer such incriminatory questions, however, you have a further right, and that is that anything you would state in answering such incriminatory questions because we have compelled you to answer those questions, will not be used against you in any subsequent proceedings that could be taken or might be taken against you. Unless, of course, we are talking of proceedings for perjury. In that case, what you would have stated could be used against you. Have I made myself clear enough for you, to you, to understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, the next thing, Mr. McCloskey will go first. He has a few, very few, questions for you. He will then be followed by some or more of the Defence teams. Mr. McCloskey, I understand you don't have a summary. I think at the end of the day we could live with that, but there are other requirements under paragraph (A) of Rule 92 ter, which need to -- particularly subparagraph (3) which you need to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Good morning, Mr. Ristanovic. Can you state your name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Cvijetin Ristanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And do you recall testifying here in The Hague in this Tribunal on 1 December 2003 in the Blagojevic/Jokic case?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And yesterday, did you have a chance to listen to your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you attest today that that testimony is accurate?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And as I told you yesterday, your testimony from that trial will be presented to this -- or has been presented to this Court. I won't have any more questions for you. But Defence counsel might.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your Honour, just as a brief outline, Mr. Ristanovic was a member of the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade and was ordered to take part in the excavations near Orahovac and the excavations at Branjevo, and that's the subject matter of his testimony. Thank you, and I don't have anything further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Now, before I pass you on to the first Defence team for your cross-examination, I also wanted to confirm to you that the Prosecution asked on your behalf for facial distortion as a protective measure to hide your identity to an extent. You enjoyed the same protective measure in Blagojevic. None of the Defence teams objected to that, and so we have granted you facial distortion, and that means that no one would be able to see your face outside the four walls -- actually, there are more, but I would still call them four walls of this courtroom. I hope you have had this explained to you before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the Defence team that seems to require most time is the Pandurevic team.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Not any more, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. You have reduced it from one hour to 15 minutes now. Okay. So then I'll go by the roster. Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, we will not cross-examine this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think he's going to break the record. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, we had put down 15 minutes and we may have some questions and we may not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you have questions, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I have no questions right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You're not closing the door completely. It's leaving it a little bit ajar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, I'm not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Nikolic Defence team? Ms. Nikolic? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Ristanovic.

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I am representing Mr. Drago Nikolic here. I'd like to ask you a few questions that have to do with your testimony before this Court in the Blagojevic case on the 1st of December 2003. If I have understood things correctly, after you received the order to go to Orahovac, you set off together with your colleague and you loaded the machine on the lorry, you arrived in Orahovo about 1300 hours on the 14th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was 1300 hours. Perhaps it was in the morning. I didn't say it was at 1300 hours exactly. Perhaps it was noon or in the morning, but around that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So we could agree that it was around noon?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You briefly stopped in front of the school because of the traffic and you saw some soldiers there, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There were some members of the police platoon among them; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It says the police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is a translation mistake, I thank my colleague. I'll repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The question was, several was several members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you didn't see which unit these military policemen belonged to, did you?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You then continued towards Krizevici, you arrived at the turn off from the main road and saw the water point, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you stay there for a while? Was there something you were waiting for?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did wait there for a while. We did stay there for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you notice troops there on the field?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: We stopped on the road. By the road there were troops, on the field there were troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And that was the beginning of the afternoon on that day; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, most likely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You were then ordered, and you received instructions, as far as I have understood from your testimony, you were ordered by Slavko Bogicevic to go under the rails towards the field to go under the flyover and that's where you were to excavate?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you went there and you worked there until about 1600 hours, when another engineer replaced you?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you arrived there, before you even started operating your machine, you noticed some troops up there in the field; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean on the other side after I had passed by the flyover?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: There were some troops, not many. I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But you didn't know which unit they belonged to; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After a while, the first lorries carrying detainees started arriving. When you saw the lorries, did you notice the escorts, namely vehicles carrying soldiers with open doors and troops inside ready to intervene in case of an attempt to escape? Did you see anything like that?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the lorries arrived, I was told to turn off the engine and to turn my back on the whole scene so I couldn't see any escorts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What about later that day? Did you notice anything?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After 1600 hours, when the other engineer replaced you, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was 1600 hours. It was the afternoon. That's all I know. I didn't have a watch. Don't try to pin me down on the hour. Whether it was 4.00 p.m. or later or earlier, I don't know. When he came, he took over the machine, continued to work. I went down to the fountain to wash my face, brought him some water.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I read this hour, 4.00 p.m., in your statement, and I seem to have heard it from the summary of your testimony. I'm sorry, so you spent that part of the afternoon between the fountain and the location where the other engineer was busy?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In all that time that you spent there, and I understood from your testimony that it was almost dark when you left the execution site, you did not receive any food, and nobody from the barracks brought you any food, refreshment, juice?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the course of that day, which I believe was a very hard day for you, I understand from your interview and your testimony that among all those troops you had seen on the execution site, you did not see any members of the military police, did you?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see any members of the military police there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You mean you saw them only outside the school in Orahovac, correct?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the course of that day, in your location on that execution site, did you notice that any officers of the Zvornik Brigade came to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: None of the officers from the Zvornik Brigade that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You did not see Drago Nikolic, the Zvornik Brigade's security officer there either?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not know Drago Nikolic before. I had never encountered him. He had never issued me any orders so I didn't know the man. So I can't tell whether he was there or not. I cannot confirm either way, because I didn't know the man at the time and I didn't meet him even later, nor did I get any orders from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Since you stayed there almost until that night, in one meadow or the other one, did you observe the incident when a child about ten years of age was found, having survived the execution?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about that incident?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but only a month, maybe a month and a half, later.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know, did you hear, about who transported that child later away from there?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ristanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Madam Nikolic. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. One moment. Is something wrong?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague warned me about the transcript, namely about page 13, line 2, the word "Zvornik" is missing, who transported the child from the site to Zvornik later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you for pointing that out, Ms. Nikolic. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder before I ask the witness any questions whether the screen could be arranged so that he and I could see one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I can figure out -- that could be a problem. Is it better?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ristanovic. I'm going to ask you just a few questions on behalf of Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I suppose as an excavator operator, you were able to operate a number of different machines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And also, you were able to identify, to recognise, different machines that were used in excavations?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I don't understand your question. What kind of excavation do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll come to the point. When you went to the site at Orahovac, the machine that you operated there was a BGH 700, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The excavator G 700.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that was a machine that was owned by the Zvornik road company; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it's your clear recollection that that was the machine you operated on that day and no other?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: 100 per cent certain, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, at that site, on the day you were there, there was one other machine, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know which of the two days I spent in that location you mean, day 1 or day 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, the other machine that you believe to have been there when you were there was a ULT 200, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: That was day 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And to your knowledge, the Zvornik Brigade did not own a ULT 200, did it?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It didn't have one. Machines were occasionally requisitioned as required.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, when machines were provided with fuel, records were kept of that, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. The machines were provided together with fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it's probably easier if I just show you some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if we could have put into e-court P300 to start off with, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ristanovic, you can probably just about read on that screen that that is what's known as a vehicle work log. Have you seen a document like that before?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that vehicle -- that vehicle work log relates to a machine called a Rovokopac; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: From what I'm able to see, and the copy is not very good, it does say Rovokopac backhoe excavator. There is an indication of the model and type. I cannot make out all the letters so... I cannot see the make and the type.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that's a machine as well as being a backhoe excavator that ran on wheels rather than on Caterpillar tracks, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's a machine on wheels that is self-propelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Unlike the BGH 700 which you've talked about which is a machine that ran on Caterpillar tracks and needed to be transported on a lorry?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, what we see on page 1 of this document, and the document in its original form would have been like a book, wouldn't it, but on page 1, we see records of that machine being fueled?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we can see here that on the 14th of July, that this machine was apparently given 40 litres of fuel. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree about the quantity but I'm not sure about the date. It is July but whether it's really 14 -- yes, now you can see when it's enlarged, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the signature on that document would be the signature of the person who, as it were, provided the fuel for the vehicle, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Most probably, although I don't know whose signature that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that. Can we now go to page 2 of this vehicle? Now, this is where the records of what the vehicle was used for are recorded on the document. Can you see that? And can it be blown up a little bit so that you can see it a bit clearer? And this is a record that the driver would keep. He would write it in the document and he would sign it. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: That's the way it should be, according to regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, can we go all the way to the far right of the document, please? This is a vehicle which is said to have been driven by you. Is that your signature? Thank you. Mr. McCloskey is going to show you the original which would be very, very helpful. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I wonder if you would go back to the front page, where it shows the provision of fuel, and see if you can compare the two signatures, because they look like they are the same signature. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: It looks the same but I cannot be 100 per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Should they, according to regulations, be signed by the same person, the provision of fuel and the record of the journeys taken?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: In the line where the -- which concerns the provision of fuel, the signature of the operator is in the last column, whereas the user's signature is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, just confirm for us, would you, that the -- that that document shows that this vehicle was supposed to have been at Orahovac on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this warrant says it was in Orahovac. It says Orahovac and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It also suggests that you were the driver. Were you driving a vehicle like that in Orahovac on the 14th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I have already stated that I was working with the backhoe loader, G 700. I did not work with this backhoe excavator.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was a machine of this description in Orahovac on the 14th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, 1995, I didn't see any machine but the G 700 I was working on, I was operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder if we could ask you to just look at another document, please, which is P301. And this document, in e-court, is backwards so we are going to have to look at page 2 first. And if -- if Mr. McCloskey could be so kind as to find the original again? Now, here, can we have again a look at the entry for the 14th of July? Firstly, can you confirm for us that this document relates to a Rovokopac torpedo? And again it's a vehicle of which you are said to be the driver.

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a backhoe excavator, torpedo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we have a look at the provision of fuel to this vehicle for the 14th of July, please? Before we move on, this again is a vehicle that runs on wheels rather than on a Caterpillar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That too is a backhoe excavator on wheels, which can go only up to a certain distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, again, 14th of July, this vehicle appears to have been provided with 40 litres of fuel.

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And again, the signature, same one we saw on the other document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: It's similar. I'm not quite sure it's exactly the same. Yes, there are lots of points of resemblance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's go to page 1 of this document, please. Again, it is said that this vehicle was in Orahovac on the 14th of July. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, were you driving a wheeled Rovokopac torpedo in Orahovac on the 14th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was operating a Caterpillar G 700.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so far as you were aware, was any such vehicle in Orahovac on the 14th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it that day, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, just before we go across to the signatures, looking at that document, it all appears to be in the same handwriting and the same pen, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does he need to answer that question? He's not a handwriting expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's a fair comment, Mr. President, I'll move on. Can we go across to the far right of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And there is that signature again, five times. Does it appear to you to be the same signature we've seen on both of those documents and on the other page of this document?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say with 100 per cent certainty. It looks the same. Whether it's 100 per cent the same, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's not your signature, is it?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, can we now go to P302, please? And this is a vehicle work log that relates to a ULT 220 and we can see at the top of the document that it's a vehicle that belongs to Birac holdings; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the driver is said to be Veljko Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, whether it's Kovacevic. I can not see the first letter on this copy. It is Veljko. Could be a K. Could be a --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you know, don't you, that Veljko Kovacevic was not a member of the Zvornik Brigade, he was somebody that was employed by the building company?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we just go to page 2 of this document, please? And just go to look at the signatures. Well, again, looks like the same signature we've seen on all these documents, both as driver and fuel provider, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: I've told you once before that I'm not an expert. There is a resemblance, but whether it's the same signature or not, I cannot assert one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it certainly doesn't look like it says "Kovacevic," does it?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN RISTANOVIC
utterances.text: It's an abbreviated signature. I cannot tell whose signature it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you ever seen the signature of the chief of engineering, Dragan Jevtic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's -- Dragan Jokic is the chief of engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not going to even bother answering that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you ever seen the signature of Dragan Jevtic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the objection stands. It's an important distinction between the commander of the engineering company and the chief of engineering. It's a crucial thing. It's not something to be set aside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can sort this out without any much ado. Forget the capacity in which this Dragan Jevtic operated, whether he was the chief of this or the chief of that or whether he was the chief of anything, for that matter. Do you know Dragan Jevtic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with his signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You can move on, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to sit down. Thank you very much, Mr. Ristanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope I haven't stopped you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, you haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That basically does the round. What I have -- I haven't asked you, Mr. Lazarevic, or Mr. Stojanovic, because you had indicated no intention to cross-examine this witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours. We said we wouldn't be examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you so much, Mr. Stojanovic. Is there re-examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Ristanovic, that means that you are finished with your testimony. You almost broke the record. Less than one hour. You are free to go. Our staff will assist you. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence, and also I would like to wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, we have a list which, as you know, is subject to a 92 bis motion. Some of these exhibits were already accepted into evidence. Just out of an abundance of caution we have listed everything that he referred to in his testimony so you would have it all, with the exception of one document which we didn't use that was also the subject of the 92 bis motion, that mentioned accused Pandurevic, but we didn't use it, and we stand by the Court's decision to redact that portion of his testimony. But we have listed here the -- all the items that were referred to in his testimony in the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can I have a copy of that, please? All right. This has been circulated. You can drop -- you have received a copy of this list, I suppose? Any objections to any of these documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? We hear none. So they are so admitted. Defence teams? Mr. Haynes, would you like to tender --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think all the documents I used are on the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Anyone else wishes to tender any documents? None? All right. That closes that chapter. And we can prepare for the next witness. So with this witness also, we are going to put in place the facial distortion. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, he would also need a caution, the same situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we can leave the curtains down for the time limit until he walks in and finds his place. Is the other witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, did -- I'm not trying to impute any fault on your part but I'm just inquiring, did you indicate that there was no need to bring this witness before 11.00 this morning? Because apparently that's what the understanding is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is a mistake. I knew that this witness would be very short and we -- Ms. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- transmitted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do it. I told you I'm not trying to put any blame on you because this -- there could have been a misunderstanding in the first place. What I suggest we do is -- we can deal with the Borovcanin interview matter now, then have the break after, at 10.30 or something like that. In the meantime the witness would have arrived by the end of the break. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's been the intention of the Prosecution to play the audiotape of the Borovcanin interview and it was my understanding from our last brief discussion on that, that was understood and that the Defence would be making various challenges at the time of the playing of it, both perhaps before and after. In my continuing discussions with Mr. Lazarevic, he has clarified for me the position that he is objecting to the playing of the interview at all, and so I would then turn over the floor to Mr. Lazarevic so that we can discuss that issue, to get to the bottom of the issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours, and good morning. Following Trial Chamber's suggestion to discuss this issue between the Prosecution and the Defence, I had a meeting together with my colleagues with Mr. McCloskey yesterday and I believe I clarified our position to Mr. McCloskey and I would like to make some additional arguments before the Trial Chamber. Basically Mr. McCloskey put it the right way. We object to the playing of the tapes for a couple of reasons. During our discussion yesterday, Mr. McCloskey told me that his intention is to play some portions of this tape in court. And first my concern as Defence counsel, was whether this portion would be taken out of context of the interview and so far, Mr. McCloskey has not indicated which portion of the interview he intends to play. I have to say before I receive such information from Mr. McCloskey, I won't be able to say whether my -- our portion remains the same or it changes. On the other hand, during these couple of days, and I must say it takes more than a month since we were working on this, we were able to reach one very, very workable transcript of this interview and although it might not sound, well, logical, but this transcript is far more accurate than the tape itself because it contains 100 per cent of everything that is said, while, when playing the tape some portions are missing, there are some pieces of interview which were not translated, some pieces were changed in translation, so the transcript that we will deal with is far more accurate than the tape itself. My concern in my discussion with Mr. McCloskey yesterday was another, and I told to Mr. McCloskey that my concern is that if we play this tape and we get an interpretation from the interpreters' booth, we will have another version of the transcript but he assured me that instead of this, we will use this transcript that we have. So then my question was what is the use, what would be the practical use of playing the tape when we will just listen to words of Mr. Borovcanin and read the transcript? I don't see the benefit the Trial Chamber might have of listening of Mr. Borovcanin speaking in B/C/S while they have the transcript in front of themselves and read it to it. So it is my suggestion to proceed with transcript and that we use only the transcript in the course of Mr. Alistair Graham in giving evidence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey? Is there a particular reason why you wish to run this audiotape, when there seems to be even 100 per cent agreement on the part of the Defence about the preciseness of the transcript? What difference would it make to you if the transcript of the tape is admitted together with the tape, without the need to have parts, portions, of the tape played in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, the Prosecution feels that actually hearing the tape is an important part of understanding and fully appreciating the interview and what is said. There are admissions made, there are other statements made, that I think hearing the tone of voice, hearing the way the interview was carried out, this is the best way to fully, in our view, to fully grasp the import of the interview as opposed to a transcript. Now, this is the historical adversarial Prosecutor in me, I must admit. I'm used to live testimony or actual testimony for the Judges to hear as opposed to a dossier. But especially if there is any kind of a challenge to the voluntariness of the interview or whatever kind of challenge there may be made to the interview, I think it's important to hear the whole thing. The other question arises, if you would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The whole thing or portions of it? Because it seems from what Mr. Lazarevic said that you -- audio, it's not a video one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's just audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's just audio, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I take it that it's partly in English when the investigator is putting questions that are then translated to Mr. Borovcanin and he is answering in his own language, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. And as Mr. Lazarevic said, in any normal situation like this, sometimes the interpreter doesn't get everything. Every once in a while, they miss -- do a misinterpretation, and we've managed to work with him to get those points pointed out so that you see in brackets when something is missed so that you will understand that I may have asked a question to Mr. Borovcanin which might have been slightly different than the question he was answering because of the translation. You'll be able to read that and hear it and understand it at the same time, where things were missed out. It doesn't happen a lot but I think we both sides felt it was significant. And regarding portions of it, my initial thoughts with Mr. Lazarevic was that we would try to reduce the air time of this to what the Prosecution felt was the most important and what the Defence felt was most important so that we might combine a "best of" audiotape and if there was any question from the Defence on -- I would -- about that, we would play the whole thing. So that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long is the whole tape? The entire tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was an interview that lasted for three days. Well, there was a one-day interview and then a two-day interview. I'm told 15 hours, though it's hard to get -- actually gauge the actual time. It's a fairly long time. That's why I was seeing if we could reduce that and perhaps delete some of the repetitiveness or the less important material. That, Mr. Lazarevic said that he was of course willing to talk to me about but he would first like to hear your ruling on whether or not you wanted to hear the tape at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How come it wasn't videotaped?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Videotape? Well, that's a good question for the investigator but I was involved in that decision and I can tell you that we -- audiotape was fine according to the rules and videotape is a much more awkward process, and it was just simpler to do an audiotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any further remarks from you, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, just very briefly, and I believe that Mr. McCloskey has just elaborated on my concerns. This is what I am worried about, the "best of." The best picture that the Trial Chamber could get on the interview is to get a whole one. By selecting certain portions, it might lead to some, well, misunderstanding of certain part of Mr. Borovcanin's interview, and furthermore, if we are going to play these 15 hours and Mr. Borovcanin said, I would really like to raise the issue of procedural economy when we already have a transcript of all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, but there is still the point raised by Mr. McCloskey in answering the question that I put to him: Is there a reason why you would not be happy with merely having the agreed-upon transcript tendered into evidence and leaving it at that? And he's given his own reasons. And I suppose you need or you should address those reasons because they are put forward against your submission that having the transcript and the transcript alone should suffice. I think that's the first thing you need. Because there are three options in my mind at the moment. One is not having the audio recording played at all, and admitting instead -- I mean it would be tendered in case we need to listen to it later on, but we would have the transcript in our own language, the language that we understand, and that should suffice for the time being. That's option number 1. Option number 2 is have portions determined, chosen, by Mr. McCloskey, with or without consultation with you, and they will be played here in the courtroom and that would address also the economy of time, plus the more relevant parts, maybe, of this interview. And the third option is to have the entire audio recording played here in this courtroom. Which would include the more and less, and the not important parts all put together. These are the three options that I see. And I suggest you tell us exactly what your position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour. The first solution is our preference, that only transcript are to be used during the evidence of Mr. Alistair Graham. We have no problems with audiotapes being distributed to the Trial Chamber and if Your Honours deem it important, they have the opportunity to listen to it but the transcript should be the document that we will operate during this cross-examination, submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't answered the point raised by Mr. McCloskey, namely that there are excerpts in this audio recording which are revealing, according to him, to important issues that he has mentioned anyway, I don't need to repeat them. Admitting the transcript -- if he's got any validity in that statement, admitting the transcript would mean -- would be tantamount to depriving him from bringing forward this element of proof. What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I'm not suggesting that if once the Trial Chamber decided to admit this into evidence, I'm not saying that the audiotapes should not be also part. I just -- I'm just trying to explain my situation. There is nothing in these tapes that is not already contained in the transcript. If Mr. McCloskey is arguing that there is something in Mr. Borovcanin's voice that might suggest that he was -- or anything like this, I have no problem of the Trial Chamber receiving the tapes. I'm just suggesting that we use just the transcript in order to save time, to be more precise and accurate during the examination of Mr. Alistair Graham.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further final submissions on your part, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly, listening to the tape, you will, for better or for worse, get to know a bit about the parties, the questions the answers, the personalities, the tone. You'll learn much more about the person and when you're looking at the issue of intent, what is in someone's mind, I think it's very important to get that feeling for the person being interviewed and if the Prosecution is being challenged for various things, the -- where the Prosecution is coming from so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. One final question to you. Have you already identified these portions that you intend showing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have not. That was something we were hoping to do with Mr. Lazarevic so that we could try to agree to something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And how soon can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think in the next -- well, we are going to have a couple of days, it appears, so we can do that in two days, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Judge Prost has a question. You will soon find out to whom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Meek, you can stand up again because it is a question for you, actually. This is on an entirely separate issue but related to the interview. When this issue was raised initially, unfortunately Mr. Ostojic is not here, but I understood his position to be that it is open to the other accused, other than Mr. Borovcanin, to challenge the admissibility of this statement in terms of matters such as its voluntariness, whether the interview was conducted in accordance with the rules and matters of that nature. Can you clarify if that is your position, that it is open to other accused to challenge the admissibility on that basis as opposed to simply challenging whether or not the statement, once admitted, is admissible with reference to the other accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They may be two separate issues, obviously. The jurisdiction where I practice, when we have an accused -- a multi-accused trial like this, Mr. Lazarevic's client has made a statement, the Prosecution wants to bring that statement in, and included in that statement are statements about other co-accused, the statement was given long after the events of the conspiracy or joint criminal enterprise have ended, normally, the accused who wants to suppress that statement would file a motion to suppress the statement and there would be a hearing as to whether or not the statement is even admissible. However, at this point, there has been no written motion filed on behalf of Mr. Borovcanin, although we've understood that there would be a challenge to the admissibility of this statement by the accused who made the statement, his lawyers. So now we are in a predicament that we believe, and I just found this out yesterday, speaking with my learned colleague, Mr. McCloskey, that in fact, when the investigator, Alistair Graham comes, that they intend to put the interview, the transcript and the tape and play it, okay? This is again, to take the words of Judge Agius, wouldn't this in fact by admitting this transcript, wouldn't it be tantamount to depriving other accused of their basic fundamental right to cross-examine their accusers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: I understand those arguments and I imagine we are going to hear those arguments ultimately, but my question to you is, is it open to Mr. Beara or to other accused to challenge the admissibility of the statement in terms of matters such as voluntariness and compliance with the rules as opposed to the separate question of whether that statement, if admitted, is then evidence against the other accused. I simply want to know your positions. I don't want to argue the matter today. I simply need that clarified, because it will obviously affect matters in terms of this witness testimony. That's all I'm seeking at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, in this Tribunal, the jurisprudence, that we would have the right to do that. However, Mr. McCloskey has already indicated, I believe that last week, that his position is we could have no standing because it's not our client's statement. However, just assume, Judge Prost, that the Bench allowed us to do that. It would be a little difficult since, unless Mr. Borovcanin would allow us extensive interview to explain all the circumstances which we're not necessarily aware of and we are not in a really good position to raise maybe all the issues that his counsel could raise in such a motion, but I believe that we could. Whether we would do with a good job, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. That answers my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. This is an interesting issue, and the -- I'd like to -- I think on the standing issue, I think there are some -- there are some challenges that other counsel in my view do not have standing to challenge and those would be those very particular to Mr. Borovcanin, such as whether he felt threatened or certain aspects of the voluntariness of the confession, for some of the reasons that Mr. Meek pointed out, though I would not close the door on their ability to challenge it in other ways, because we will be offering this statement against all the accused for any purposes that you deem it be necessary, and that is different than the jurisdiction that my learned friend made a reference to, and if that is the case, if that is your decision -- as you know, this is a decision that's being currently dealt with in the other two big cases, whether or not a co-accused's statement can be used against others. If that's the case, then there may be other areas that other Defence counsel do have standing on that are less related to the personal aspect of an interview. Perhaps such as whether it was done according to the rules or not. That sort of thing. And so I wouldn't argue that they don't have standing on all issues. There may be an issue that they do have standing for because this statement could very well be used against them as well. And so I wouldn't argue that in a pure common law sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. One last thing before we break. Yesterday, I think you were here, Mr. McCloskey, I referred to the Nikolic motion requesting an order from this Trial Chamber to the Prosecution to urgently disclose all Rule 68 material in relation to Witnesses PW 108 and 102. You will recall what I stated yesterday, that we are not here to spend our time reminding you of what the rules say in relation to your respective duties, and we said that this matter can be resolved through a dialogue which we expected you yesterday to have between yourselves and then you come back to us with a final solution. We haven't heard from you or from the Beara or Nikolic teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did have a discussion with Ms. Nikolic and we brought Julian Nichols into that discussion and we did explain what we had done in search of the materials, and we continue to talk with them and are open to any other searches or specific items they are looking for. So we have talked. I'm not sure Ms. Nikolic and Mr. Nicholls came to any agreement but we are open for any further discussions on that, and I don't believe we agreed to disagree on anything. I think we were still discussing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. We'll have the break now. Perhaps you can have a final discussions and then come back to us soon after the -- we resume after the break. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just wanted to have something for the record. Following Your Honour's ruling we shall file a motion on Thursday and we shall object to Prosecution request to add Mr. Borovcanin's interviews on the rule 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't recall having ever said that we require you to do this, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was in response to the Prosecution motion. You ruled on this yesterday. You ordered us to file a response by Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, that's another matter. All right. Okay, okay, okay, okay. That's another matter. Okay. That's -- I thought you were still referring to -- okay. We weren't on the same frequency. Yes, exactly. We were not on the same frequency. We will have a 25-minute break. But, please, you need -- he's here? All right. So we'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Stanojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish -- and my colleagues, I wish to welcome you to this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're about to start giving evidence very soon. Before you do so, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration, equivalent to an oath, that in the course of your testimony you'll be speaking the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud and that's your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are a few other things I wish to explain to you. Number 1 is that the Prosecution has asked on your behalf to have in place one protective measure, which supposedly you know about already, and that is facial distortion. In other words, we have granted this protective measure which you enjoyed before when you testified here, and that would make it impossible for outsiders, persons outside this courtroom, to be able see your face. What they will see is a combination of different coloured cubes or squares. That's number 1. Number 2 is a matter of great importance, and it relates to one's right against being forced to incriminate himself. What am I referring to? I'm referring to a right that you have as a witness, in case you are asked questions which, if answered truthfully, could tend to incriminate you. Just as it is in many countries, we also have a rule that gives protection, extends protection to this right, and this right being your right, in case such questions are put to you, to ask the Trial Chamber to exempt you from answering such questions on the basis that they are -- the answer to them could expose you to criminal proceedings. As I said, this is a right, but like many other rights, it's not an absolute one. Because whether you actually will answer such questions or not will depend on our decision, and we may grant you exemption, but we may also do exactly the opposite, after hearing your submissions, of course, and those of parties, and compel you to give -- to answer such incriminatory questions. If we do compel you to answer such questions, however, whatever you state in replying to such incriminatory questions cannot be used later on in any proceedings that might be taken against you, unless, of course, these proceedings are on perjury, false testimony, in other words. Did I make my explanation clear enough for you to understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Third thing, there will be a few questions from Mr. McCloskey who will then be followed by some of the Defence teams. I think all the Defence teams, for the time being. And after that -- hopefully we'll finish today, after that, you will be free to go. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stanojevic. Can you first for the record tell us your name?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ostoja Stanojevic, born on the 13th of August, 1947.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall testifying here in this Tribunal back on the 4th and 5th of December 2003?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the last day or so, have you had a chance to listen to your testimony in that trial?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And today, can you attest that that testimony was accurate?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. As I mentioned to you yesterday, I won't have any further questions for you. We will stand on your testimony. But others may have questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, Mr. Stanojevic was a truck driver for the Zvornik Brigade engineering company and was assigned to go down and help clean up Srebrenica and was then assigned to clean up bodies at the Kravica warehouse and transport them to the grave at Glogova. That's a very brief synopsis. Thank you, and I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I've got all the Defence teams here wishing to cross-examine the witness. I'll start with Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We will not cross-examine him, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: As with the other witness, Your Honour, I don't believe I have any questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence of Mr. Nikolic will not cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Mr. Lazarevic or Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we had announced that we would need 15 minutes for cross-examination. I now believe it will take less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stanojevic. My name is Miodrag Stojanovic and together my colleagues in the team, we appear for Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin. I would only like to ask you a few questions related to your knowledge and your recollection of what happened in Kravica when you got there. If I'm not mistaken, from reading your statement, in the chronology of events, you were sent on the 14th of July from Zvornik to report to the civilian Defence in the municipality of Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Therefrom, together with the people from the civilian defence of Zvornik municipality, you left for Bratunac municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, what time of day was it on the 14th of July when you arrived at Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon. I couldn't tell you the exact time. It could have been 3.00 p.m. or 4.00 p.m. I know that I had arrived at the civilian defence of Zvornik at noon, stayed there for about an hour or two, and it was later in the afternoon that we arrived at Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it is possible to reach Bratunac from Zvornik using two routes. One would be via Drinjaca, Konjevic Polje, then to the left via Kravica and Glogova to Bratunac, and the other route would be from Drinjaca along the Drina River to reach Bratunac again, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember whether on that day, on the 14th of July in the afternoon, as you just said, you took the route along the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: One section of the road is macadam and you had to go more slowly?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a macadam road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That afternoon of the 14th, you were not involved in any activities, you didn't have a particular job to do?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, in the morning, you were again in Bratunac because you had spent that night in Bratunac town itself?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was only in the afternoon that you were given the assignment to move, together with the people from the civilian defence of Bratunac, towards Kravica, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You have already explained what you did in the afternoon, and you explained who was engaged in that activity. Will you agree with me that on that 15th of July, in the afternoon, outside the warehouse in Kravica, you did not see members of the police, the MUP, anywhere?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any troops or policemen that day while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The job involving the loading of bodies was performed by members of the civilian defence wearing protective coveralls?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were from the civilian defence. They had their working outfit consisting of top and bottoms. Whether they were the public utilities service or the civilian defence, I don't know to this day. I've already explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us again who was the person who gave you your orders what to do?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any orders. There was a man who had come with us, who came to fetch me, and told me I had a job to do in Kravica. I told him I don't know where Kravica is. He said, "I'll come with you." And then he really accompanied me and he did the same job up there with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you had -- you made two trips to Glogova and to Kravica, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, when you were outside the warehouse in Kravica, did you at any point see any killings outside the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said you didn't see any troops or police. Let me put the question more broadly: Did you perhaps see any uniformed persons outside the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, can you tell us now when you took off driving those bodies from the warehouse towards Glogova, can you remember whether you took a right turn or a left turn looking in the direction of Bratunac towards the site where they were buried?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: When I was going down the slope towards Glogova, I took a right turn and there was another 300 metres to the site, so in fact when I took a turn, I went practically backwards for about 100 metres and then there is a house there, before I reached the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me finish with this question: While you were working that day, on the 15th July, in the afternoon, you did not hear or find out at any point that there were some other graves on the left-hand side of the road looking towards Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The night of the 15th of July you also spent in Bratunac, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of July, in the morning, you went back to Zvornik because you no longer wished or needed to continue to do the job that you were invited for?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: There was nothing for me to do there because on Sunday we were supposed to go to Srebrenica. However, when we found out, when Rajko found out, that the troops from Srebrenica emerged on the confrontation line at Baljkovica and many of them got killed there, then Rajko and I agreed to go home. He had a lot of family on the confrontation line so we decided on Sunday to go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Going back, did you again go along the Drina River or did you take the other route via Konjevic Polje and Drinjaca?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Via Konjevic Polje. I didn't want to take the macadam road again because I was told by people who knew those things that the other road was shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that 16th of July, driving on the road from Bratunac towards Konjevic Polje and Drinjaca, did you see any executions along the road, any killings, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In conclusion, can you tell us when you returned to Zvornik, what time of day it was?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps 8.00 or 9.00. I don't know exactly. We took breakfast, Rajko went to the municipality, then the time it took me to go to the truck, then he came back and told me the story. I told him, "Let's you and I agree on something. I wouldn't like to go to Srebrenica. Let's go home instead." He was of the same opinion so we set off. Perhaps 9.00, 10.00. I don't know. At any rate, it was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, both you and I know which Rajko you mean but could you explain it for the record? Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Rajko Djokic, an employee of the civilian defence. He was in civilian clothes. There were three of them on that trip. I already enumerated them. The other two left the same night for Zvornik while Rajko and I stayed the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stanojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these were all my questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. The Borovcanin team is ready? Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Gvero Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Likewise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Pandurevic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Mr. Stanojevic, my name is Djordje Sarapa, and I appear for -- Dragan Jokic told you to go with your truck to the civilian defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: After you reported to the civilian defence in Zvornik, all the orders, including where you were to go and what you were to do, were given to you by people from the civilian defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, as soon as I reported to the civilian defence, they had authority over me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So it was exclusively people from the civilian defence who told you where to go and what to do?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: They told us we were going to Bratunac, but I took the shorter route along the Drina. Maybe I'm not understanding the question correctly, but they didn't tell me which route to take. I listened to my colleagues who knew the terrain and told me there was a shorter route towards Bratunac, to save fuel, I took the left side along the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I didn't mean how you should travel, but they told you your destination, where you should go with your truck. It was the civilians from the civilian defence who told you that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Before that, when Major Jokic told me that I was going to Srebrenica for the clearing and that I was to stay for 10 days, he said there was a lot of rubbish and to report to the civilian defence, and when I reported to the civilian defence, I had to take my cue from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to establish. When you reported to the civilian defence in Zvornik, all further orders were given to you by them?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of the other person from civilian defence that was with you during in this -- these couple of days?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You mean the worker who came to fetch me or you mean Rajko Djokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned a person name Dragan Mirkovic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Dragan Mirkovic and another Sekonjic [phoen]. Rajko Djokic and Sekonjic [phoen] were with me in the truck, whereas Dragan came in his own truck. They were there in the civilian defence already and when they were going home, they came to accompany me to my truck saying that us -- saying that the two of us, Rajko and I were staying, whereas Arsen and others left to go home the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mirkovic tell you who he was getting his orders from?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
